title: Expansionary and Contractionary Fiscal Policy
short: Raising spending or cutting taxes pushes AD right to close a recessionary gap; the reverse closes an inflationary gap.
trouble: Students choose a tax increase to fight a recession, or count transfer payments as government purchases (transfers work like a tax cut).

blocks.html: A demand shock can leave the economy in a gap. Fiscal policy is the government's use of spending and taxes to push aggregate demand back toward full employment. Its strength depends on the multipliers.

Expansionary fiscal policy (more government purchases, lower taxes, or higher transfer payments) shifts AD right to close a recessionary gap. Contractionary fiscal policy (fewer purchases, higher taxes, lower transfers) shifts AD left to close an inflationary gap. In the United States, Congress and the President set fiscal policy.

Government purchases are part of AD directly. Taxes and transfers change households' disposable income, and so consumption. In a recession, too little spending leaves workers and factories idle; adding spending (or leaving households more to spend) moves output toward potential. In an inflationary gap, the economy is straining; trimming spending eases the pressure on prices.

blocks.title: Choosing a policy
blocks.q: Unemployment is high and output is below potential. Which fiscal policies fit?
steps: This is a recessionary gap: AD must shift right.
Raise government purchases, cut taxes, or raise transfer payments. Real GDP and the price level rise; unemployment falls.

blocks.title: Purchases or transfers?
blocks.q: The government raises Social Security payments by \$30 billion. Is that an increase in G?
steps: No. Social Security checks buy no good or service: they are transfer payments.
They raise households' income, so they work like a tax cut, through consumption, with the smaller tax-style multiplier.
blocks.a: No: a transfer, which works like a tax cut

blocks.html: Discretionary fiscal policy has practical limits: it takes time to see a recession, pass a law and spend the money, and a change may arrive after the economy has already recovered. How large fiscal multipliers are, and so how much a given change helps, is debated among economists.

Choosing a tax increase to fight a recession, or counting transfer payments as government purchases. A tax increase lowers spending, which deepens a recession. Transfers are not G; they work like a tax cut. Check: in a recessionary gap, every tool should push AD right.
